name: Mariscal Sucre International Airport
before:
Ecuador's busiest airport, at Tababela about 18 km east of Quito, which is why locals often just call it Tababela.

It replaced a 53-year-old airport of the same name in February 2013 and is ten times larger, covering 1,500 hectares. It was the first airport in the Western Hemisphere to earn a five-star Skytrax rating.

It is the main hub for Avianca Ecuador and the largest hub for LATAM Ecuador. It was also the hub for TAME, the national flag carrier, until the government liquidated that airline in 2020.

Cargo is a bigger part of the picture than most passengers realise. The airport handled about 364,674 tonnes in 2024, fifth in Latin America and the Caribbean, and roughly 92 per cent of export cargo was flowers.

One routing quirk to check: KLM's Quito to Amsterdam service makes a stop in Guayaquil.

The airport is named after the independence leader Antonio José de Sucre.
after:
Ecuador's busiest airport, at Tababela, about 20 to 25 km north east of central Quito.

In February 2013 it replaced the old airport of the same name, which sat in the middle of the city. Its 1,500 hectare site is ten times larger. Skytrax rates it a five-star regional airport, the only five-star airport in Latin America and the Caribbean.

Avianca and LATAM both fly from here.

Cargo is a bigger part of the picture than most passengers realise. The airport handled about 400,000 tonnes in 2025, and flowers make up the bulk of its exports. Quiport, which runs the airport, says an ACI-LAC ranking in May 2026 put it fourth for air cargo in Latin America and the Caribbean.

The airport is named after Antonio José de Sucre.

claims.claim: Ecuador's busiest airport
claims.note: INEC's latest airport-level split (its transport bulletin of August 2025, 2024 figures from the DGAC) puts Quito first for international passengers, 53.9 per cent of arrivals and 51.2 per cent of departures, with Guayaquil next. The operator (20 February 2026) calls Quito Ecuador's main way in and out, and counted about 5.4 million passengers in 2025 (held back below). Guayaquil's own airport authority calls Guayaquil the second busiest airport in Ecuador. No 2025 airport-by-airport passenger table could be read: the DGAC's 2025 statistical bulletin is linked only through its intranet login.

claims.claim: cargo about 400,000 tonnes in 2025
claims.inAfter: The airport handled about 400,000 tonnes in 2025
claims.note: Was 'about 364,674 tonnes in 2024' (Quiport's 2024 report via Wikipedia; the operator's rectified 2024 figure is 364,000, so the old figure was right but a year stale). A cargo total replaces a cargo total. The 2025 figures differ a little by source: the DGAC 397,798.54 tonnes (its release of 29 January 2026, dated from its own news index), Quiport 402,832 (its 2025 sustainability report, July 2026), 405,024 on ACI-LAC's count as Quiport reports it and 407,000 in Quiport's preliminary figure of January 2026. 'About 400,000' is what they all support. The DGAC's figures put Guayaquil, the next airport, at 26,991.92 tonnes.

claims.claim: KLM's Quito to Amsterdam service stops in Guayaquil

Guayaquil's live boards on 23 September 2026 show KLM's KL 755 arriving from Amsterdam at 17:05 and leaving for Amsterdam at 18:35, with no Quito leg shown; BES-reporter (July 2024, more than 12 months old) says only that KLM flies between Quito, Guayaquil and Amsterdam. Quito's own flight board is on the Cloudflare-blocked passenger site and KLM's newsroom refused the link lister (503). For Andy: worth checking whether KLM still serves Quito at all, and which way the stop runs.
